sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You'll learn how to teach an AI a custom format, style, or pattern by showing it examples — without any training, configuration, or technical setup. This technique is called few-shot prompting and it's one of the fastest ways to get output that matches your specific standards.

## What "Few-Shot" Means

The word "shot" in this context means "example". So:

- **Zero-shot** — no examples given; the model works from the description alone
- **One-shot** — one example given; the model learns the pattern from that single case
- **Few-shot** — two to five examples given; the model learns a more reliable pattern

You've been using zero-shot prompting in every lesson so far. You describe what you want, and the model does its best. Zero-shot works for most tasks.

Few-shot becomes valuable when:
- You have a specific output format the model doesn't default to
- You need a consistent style that's hard to describe in words
- You're doing a classification, extraction, or transformation task where correctness matters
- The "right" output is defined by pattern, not by instruction

The key insight is this: **showing is clearer than telling**. If you need a very specific output format, showing three examples of that format conveys more information than a paragraph of description.

## A Few-Shot Prompt in Practice

Here's a concrete example. Suppose you need to write email subject lines in a specific style: short, specific, no clickbait, always starts with the recipient's context.

**Zero-shot (describe the format):**

Write a subject line for an email to a client about a delayed project.
The subject should be short, honest, and professional.

The model will produce something generic. Now watch what happens with examples:

**Few-shot (show the format):**

Write subject lines in this style. Here are examples:

Email: Telling a client their invoice is ready
Subject: Invoice #2847 ready — please review by Friday

Email: Following up on a proposal sent 2 weeks ago
Subject: Proposal follow-up — next steps for your consideration

Email: Informing a client a feature they requested won't be in this release
Subject: Feature update — scope decision for Q3 release

Now write a subject line for this email:
Email: Telling a client their project will be delayed by two weeks due to
a technical issue we discovered during testing.

The three examples establish a precise pattern: starts with the topic category, then a dash, then a specific and honest descriptor. The model now generates a subject line that matches that format — without you having to articulate the pattern in words.

**How many examples do you need?** One example is often enough to establish a format. Two to three examples show the pattern more reliably and help the model distinguish your format from similar ones. More than five examples rarely improves things and makes your prompt harder to manage.

## Where Few-Shot Prompting Shines

Few-shot is highest-value for tasks that require a consistent, repeatable output pattern:

**Text classification:**

Classify these customer messages by urgency. Examples:

Message: "My order hasn't arrived and it was due 3 days ago."
Urgency: HIGH — customer waiting, specific timeline mentioned

Message: "Do you have this product in blue?"
Urgency: LOW — product inquiry, no time pressure

Message: "I was charged twice for my last order."
Urgency: HIGH — financial error, needs immediate correction

Now classify:
Message: "Can I change the delivery address on my current order?"

Extract the key information from job postings in this format. Examples:

Posting: "We're looking for a Python developer with 3+ years of experience
in Django. Remote-friendly, competitive salary, must be based in Europe."
Output: Role: Python Developer | Experience: 3+ years | Stack: Python, Django |
Location: Europe (remote-friendly) | Salary: Not stated

Posting: "Junior React developer wanted. No experience required — we'll
train you. London office, £30k starting salary."
Output: Role: Junior React Developer | Experience: None required | Stack: React |
Location: London (on-site) | Salary: £30k

Now extract from:
Posting: "Full-stack engineer (5+ years) for fast-growing SaaS startup.
Must know Node.js and PostgreSQL. San Francisco or fully remote. $140–170k."

Write tweets in my style. Here are three I've actually posted:

"Spent 3 hours on a bug that turned out to be a missing semicolon.
Debugging is mostly archaeology."

"Your first version will be embarrassing. Ship it anyway.
The embarrassment fades. The learning doesn't."

"Every 'simple feature' has a graveyard of edge cases behind it.
Rest in peace, assumptions."

Now write a tweet about the experience of learning a new programming language.

Notice the third example: you're training the model on your real writing voice. The examples capture your rhythm, your use of metaphor, your punchline structure — none of which you could easily describe in words.

**Garbage examples produce garbage output.** If your examples are inconsistent, the model learns the inconsistency. Before you use few-shot prompting, make sure your examples actually represent the pattern you want — not a rough approximation of it.

sections.title: Teach Claude Your Format
sections.content:
Choose a formatting task you actually do — or would want to do consistently. Here are some ideas:

- Email subject lines in your preferred style
- Meeting notes in a specific structure
- Task descriptions for a project management tool
- Status update messages for your team
- Social media posts in your writing voice

Open [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai) and build a few-shot prompt:

1. Write 3 examples of the output you want. These can be real examples or invented ones that match your standard.
2. Format them consistently: show the input and the output for each example.
3. Then give Claude a new input and ask it to produce the output in the same format.

**Template:**
```
Produce [output type] in this format. Examples:

Input: [example 1 input]
Output: [example 1 output]

Input: [example 2 input]
Output: [example 2 output]

Input: [example 3 input]
Output: [example 3 output]

Now produce:
Input: [your real input]
```

Save this few-shot template to your prompt library — it's reusable every time you need that format.
**You've completed lesson 3-5.** You can now teach AI a custom output format using examples — bypassing the limitations of trying to describe in words what's easier to demonstrate.
